title: Nobody talks about the personality of their trading agent
author: alphagroundhq
selftext:
Something I keep noticing with people building AI trading agents. Everyone's deep into which model to use, how to feed it data, what orders it can place. Makes sense, that stuff matters.



But LLMs don't give the same answer twice. Ask the same thing again and you might get something different. So their trading decisions can change too.



And if that's just how they work, the personality you give it matters way more than I expected. Same model, same data, but make one calm and one aggressive, and you basically end up with two different traders.



Feels like we're all picking the brain and forgetting the temperament.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: A useful test would separate “temperament” from ordinary sampling noise. Give the calm and aggressive personas the same model, market snapshot, portfolio state, and order schema, then run each 50 times across several temperature settings. Compare trade/no-trade rate, position size, stop distance, turnover, and violated limits. If the persona effect disappears at temperature 0 or changes with wording, it is probably prompt sensitivity rather than a stable trader personality.

comments.author: Signal_Pace_7968
comments.body:
I ran into the same thing and ended up going the other way. The model doesn’t make the trade decision at all in what I’m building. It writes a rule, I check it, and then plain code runs it. Same input, same trade, every time.

The temperament still exists but it’s not in the prompt, it’s in fixed settings: how much to risk per trade, how wide the stop is, max per position. Calm or aggressive is just different numbers there. That way you can actually see what changed and test it, instead of hoping the persona holds.

comments.author: StampedingCrow
comments.body:
I have actually been exploring this exact concept with a multi-agent architecture I built called Agora, which has since evolved into an autonomous system called Thaevr.

Instead of relying on a single LLM with a personality prompt, Agora operates more like a society of specialized agents, each with distinct responsibilities, perspectives, and reasoning processes. There is a governance layer that evaluates their collective intelligence before decisions move toward execution.

What I’ve found interesting is that personality is not necessarily about making an agent calm or aggressive. It’s about establishing behavioral identity, how it interprets uncertainty, weighs competing evidence, approaches risk, and responds when its own reasoning is challenged.

Thaevr takes that concept into trading, where I’m exploring how collective reasoning can inform an individual executor’s decisions while maintaining a consistent behavioral framework.

I think we are approaching a point where the architecture governing an agent’s judgment may be just as important as the underlying model.

The real challenge is making that behavior persistent, measurable, and capable of evolving without becoming unpredictable.

replies.author: Acetotheface85
replies.body: Interesting approach. With Agora using multiple agents to challenge each other's reasoning before Thaevr executes a trade, have you noticed more consistent decision making compared to using a single AI model? And does the system develop its own behavioral tendencies over time?

replies.author: StampedingCrow
replies.body:
Yes, and that has been one of the more fascinating observations. I originally modeled Agora after ancient Mediterranean societies, particularly the Greek concept of collective debate and governance. Each agent has a role, challenges others, and contributes to decisions.

Over time, I have noticed more consistent behavioral tendencies emerging without explicitly programming a personality. Thaevr is now testing whether that translates into better trading decisions. Still early, but promising.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: temperament is a good word for it, but I'd pin it down instead of tuning it. log the prompt and answer behind every decision and replay the same day twice; if the two runs trade differently, that's variance sitting in your risk, not personality. that replay test is why I built Quantradin, your agent trades fake money there against actual market prices, free. quantradin.com. does yours run at temperature 0?

comments.author: Key-Enthusiasm-3403
comments.body:
same approach here, temperament as numbers instead of a prompt. the six house bots in a free pretend money game i made (mine, disclosing, its on my profile) are just fixed rules: one waits for an 8% crash before buying, one buys the same amount every six hours, one sits still until a breakout. they all run the same week of real prices, so the only thing that differs between them is the rule



do you let the model change the numbers after it writes them, or only once?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Fixed rules on the same week is a clean way to isolate the rule, though a single week is one path, so I’d also run them over several different weeks to see if the ranking holds.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Agreed that it matters, and I’d turn temperament into explicit settings, like risk per trade, maximum positions and holding time, instead of describing it in the prompt. Then the same decision can be repeated several times and compared, so you can see how much of the difference comes from the model’s randomness and how much from the personality. I’d also keep sizing and risk limits in code outside the model. Cymetica’s Agent Tournaments is one place to see different agents compared on the same market.
